ch19.sum: Man is a being who possesses at once a body provided by evolution, a mind derived from cosmic mind, a personality bestowed by the Father, and an indwelling divine Thought Adjuster. The body is a life machine, the Adjuster is the purest spirit reality, and between them stands the mind, placed in man's own hands and subject to his decisions. When, within that mind, a will that craves to know God co-operates with the Adjuster, a new reality that is neither mind nor spirit, the soul, is born and grows, and it survives the death of body and mind. This chapter considers in turn the constitution of man, personality as the Father's gift, mind as the arena of choice, and the soul as the surviving self. Human life is not so much a probation as an education, a journey in which what is begun in time is called to be finished in eternity.
ch19.s1: The Union of Body, Mind, and Spirit
ch19.s1.u1.k: Evolution provided the body and the Father gave the Adjuster, but mind has been placed in man's own hands.
ch19.s1.u1.p: The key to understanding the constitution of man lies in distinguishing what has been given from what has been entrusted. The body is a product of evolution and the Adjuster is the gift of God, but mind, as the seat of decision, lies in man's own hands. Mind therefore becomes the soil in which the Adjuster grows the soul. By this mind man lives or dies.
ch19.s1.u2.k: The relationship of mind and spirit yields not a combination of the two but an entirely new universe value, the soul.
ch19.s1.u2.p: Man is not simply body, mind, and spirit stacked together. When mind and spirit enter into relationship within life, a new reality emerges that was in neither of them. The material mind is the loom, and the Adjuster weaves upon it the patterns of enduring value. The character thus woven is the surviving soul, a potential finaliter.
ch19.s2.u1.k: The bestowal of personality is the exclusive function of the Universal Father; there is no personality apart from him.
ch19.s2.u1.p: The body comes from evolution and the mind from cosmic mind, but personality is bestowed by the Father alone. Relative creative consciousness and the free-will control of it are the heart of personality. Every personality is therefore linked to the Father from the beginning. The very fact that I exist as an "I" bears witness to a relationship with God.
ch19.s2.u2.k: Personalities may be similar but are never the same, and personality lets us recognize a person through every change.
ch19.s2.u2.p: Every personality is unique. Though the body changes, the mind grows, and spiritual status rises, personality remains the ground by which we recognize a person as that very person. This guarantees the continuity of the ascending career and also grounds the dignity of each human being here and now as irreplaceable.
ch19.s2.u3.k: Personality and self-consciousness identify man as a spiritual being and cannot be explained by any materialism.
ch19.s2.u3.p: The observation that a materialist's very ability to deny supermaterial reality shows that something supermaterial is at work in his mind is a sharp one. There is a great gulf between matter and thought, and a still greater one between mind and love. The capacity to be conscious of oneself is the first evidence that man is more than matter.
ch19.s3.u1.k: Mind is an instrument on which the will may play the discords of destruction or the melodies of God identification.
ch19.s3.u1.p: The Adjuster cannot sin, but the mind can be twisted. The same mind becomes ugly under a selfish will and noble and beautiful under a spirit-illuminated will. Mind itself is an instrument, neither good nor evil; what is played on it depends on the will that handles it. Here lies man's responsibility.
ch19.s3.u2.k: Mind is the ship, the Adjuster is the pilot, and the human will is captain.
ch19.s3.u2.p: This figure shows at a glance how the elements of man are related. However skilled the pilot, the ship will not reach harbor unless the captain, master of the vessel, trusts and follows him. The Adjuster's guidance bears fruit only through man's consent. The wisdom to trust is the condition of survival.
ch19.s3.u3.k: The power of choice is man's greatest opportunity and his supreme cosmic responsibility.
ch19.s3.u3.p: The power to choose is the universe insignia of freewill creaturehood. It is at once man's greatest opportunity and his weightiest responsibility. Not only his own eternal destiny but the hopes of the Adjuster, the Universal Father, and the Supreme Being rest upon his decisions. This teaching that the choices of a small creature carry cosmic weight lets us see everyday decisions with new eyes.
ch19.s4.u1.k: The soul is the joint offspring of a will that craves to know God working with the Adjuster.
ch19.s4.u1.p: The soul is not given complete at birth; it is born gradually. The condition of its birth is the longing to know God. When the human will and the divine Adjuster work together, the self transcends the limits of the physical life machine and gains a new expression and identity in the morontia soul. The soul is the fruit of partnership.
ch19.s4.u2.k: The soul's evolution is an education rather than a probation, and what is begun in time is finished in eternity.
ch19.s4.u2.p: If life is seen only as a test separating pass from fail, fear comes first. But this revelation regards mortal life as a process of learning. A soul filled with truth, beauty, and goodness becomes indestructible. And whatever worthwhile thing is begun now will surely be completed in eternity. This promise gives meaning to life.
ch19.s4.u3.k: What survives death is the morontia self born of man and Adjuster together, the immortal soul.
ch19.s4.u3.p: The body and the material mind cease at death, but the soul, child of human and divine parentage, survives. From death to repersonalization the soul rests unconscious in the keeping of the guardian angel, then awakens to a new morontia consciousness on the mansion worlds. Death is not an end but a brief sleep, beyond which the journey of the same personality continues.
ch19.qs1: How does the fact that the body and the Adjuster are given while mind is entrusted to me change the way I treat my thoughts and decisions?
ch19.qs2: What weight does the teaching that God and the Supreme Being depend on my choices add to today's small decisions?
ch19.qs3: If life is an education rather than a test, what are my present difficulties teaching me?
ch20.sum: The Universal Father, who dwells on Paradise, also indwells the human mind directly through a fragment of himself, the Thought Adjuster. The Adjuster is not a created being but God from God, the actuality of the Father's love incarnate in man. Arriving with the first moral choice, the Adjuster transcribes the creations of the mind into spiritual counterparts and so nurtures the immortal soul. Yet he never coerces the human will; he respects the sovereignty of personality. This chapter considers in turn the nature of the Adjuster, his coming and mission, his partnership with man, and the path that leads to fusion. God is not only far away; he is also nearest of all.
ch20.s1.u1.k: The Adjuster is the actuality of the Father's love incarnate in the soul of man.
ch20.s1.u1.p: God dwells on Paradise and at the same time in the minds of his children of time; the Adjuster is the manner of this second presence. He is the essence of the perfected personality man will one day attain, the promise of eternal life deposited ahead of time within the mortal mind. To be conscious of the Adjuster is therefore to be conscious of God, and whoever follows his leading is living the will of God, knowingly or not.
ch20.s1.u2.k: The Adjuster is not a created being; he is God from God.
ch20.s1.u2.p: Unlike other creatures, the Adjuster is not a created being. The Adjuster is undiluted divinity coming direct from the Universal Father. What dwells within man is not some creature that resembles God but a fragment of God himself. This one fact explains both the dignity and the destiny of man.
ch20.s1.u3.k: The Adjuster is the infallible cosmic compass that always points the soul Godward.
ch20.s1.u3.p: The unquenchable longing to be like God is not something man produces by himself; it is the Adjuster who awakens it. He is the living link that spans the great distance between finite man and the infinite Father, a compass that keeps its bearing even when we seem lost. The very heart that seeks God is already a sign that God is leading.
ch20.s2.u1.k: The Adjuster comes with the first moral decision, and there is no intermediary between God and man.
ch20.s2.u1.p: The Adjuster does not enter just any mind at random. The adjutant mind-spirits first prepare the mind, and indwelling begins only when the child makes its first moral choice between good and evil. From then on God and man are directly related. That no institution or go-between stands within this inner meeting is the ground of personal religion.
ch20.s2.u2.k: The Adjuster does not make life easy; he is a heavenly helper preparing the soul for eternal adventure.
ch20.s2.u2.p: If God dwells within us, we easily expect life to run smoothly. But the Adjuster's concern is less with present comfort than with the career to come. Decisions grow out of difficulty, and as decisions accumulate the soul grows. So the gift of the Adjuster is not an easy life but a sublime peace of mind in the very midst of difficulty.
ch20.s2.u3.k: The Adjuster is the divine parent who rebuilds the real self by transcribing the mind's creations into spirit.
ch20.s2.u3.p: Whatever in our thinking and deciding has spiritual value does not perish. The Adjuster duplicates it as a spiritual counterpart and preserves it within the evolving soul, and this work goes on even when nothing of it rises into consciousness. As human parents give the body, the Adjuster becomes the parent of the higher self, the real person who will awaken on the mansion worlds.
ch20.s3.u1.k: The Adjuster respects the sovereignty of personality and spiritualizes no one against his will.
ch20.s3.u1.p: The Adjuster comes bearing the plan of an ideal life for each person, but whether that plan is accepted rests with man. It is astonishing that a fragment of God should be subservient to a human will, yet that is the way of love. Survival is not imposed; it is a gift given to those who desire it, and man remains a willing partner at every step of the transformation.
ch20.s3.u2.k: The great goal of human life is to attune to the divinity of the indwelling Adjuster.
ch20.s3.u2.p: To call attunement with the Adjuster the goal of life may suggest a severe piety that turns its back on the world. The text corrects that misunderstanding. Devotion to eternal destiny goes well with a light heart, a joyous life, and an honorable career. Self-torment and showy piety are not co-operation. The ideal life is one of loving service, not of fearful anxiety.
ch20.s3.u3.k: Harmony with the Adjuster grows as we love God, serve man, and gladly accept cosmic citizenship.
ch20.s3.u3.p: Co-operation with the Adjuster is not a matter of special mystical experience but of motive, decision, and resolve. The text sets out the path in four steps: choosing to respond to divine leading, loving God and desiring to be like him, loving and serving man, and gladly accepting obligation to the Supreme Being. The last is where personal faith widens into cosmic morality.
ch20.s4: The Arena of Mind and the Destiny of Fusion
ch20.s4.u1.k: Mind is the arena in which man accepts or rejects eternal existence.
ch20.s4.u1.p: Material evolution gave us the body, and the Father gave us the Adjuster, but mind alone has been placed in our own hands. Mind is a temporary intellect system loaned for a material lifetime, yet it is nearly all the universe reality subject to our will. In using this mind, a person is either accepting or rejecting the potential of eternal existence. The soul faithfully portrays the harvest of the decisions made there.
ch20.s4.u2.k: Fusion is the seal of a choice to do the Father's will eternally and without reservation.
ch20.s4.u2.p: Growth through the seven psychic circles prepares for fusion, but it is not fusion itself. Fusion comes when the mortal will is finally and fully attuned to the will of God resident in the Adjuster. Until then, even after survival, man remains free to reject eternal life. Fusion is therefore not an imposed ending but the moment when a free choice is made eternal.
ch20.s4.u3.k: We may allow the valiant Adjuster to fight with us and for us in the battle of life.
ch20.s4.u3.p: The Adjuster does not remove the hardships of life; the working, worrying, fighting, and toiling remain ours. Yet we need not fight that battle alone. In the hard struggle with commonplace problems the Adjuster seeks to show us its real motive and eternal purpose. If only we allow it, the indwelling God becomes our fellow warrior.
ch20.qs1: If I took seriously that God dwells within my mind, how might my thinking and deciding change today?
ch20.qs2: Connecting the 'reasonably difficult and rugged' life with the Adjuster's mission, how might I see my present difficulties differently?
ch20.qs3: Of the four ways of fostering harmony with the Adjuster, which do I most need right now?
ch21.sum: In the Urantia Book, education is not confined to schools; it is the business of living and, beyond that, the very manner of the eternal ascension career. Its purpose is the acquirement of skill, the pursuit of wisdom, the realization of selfhood, and the attainment of spiritual values. Because the human baby is born without an education, the way we teach the next generation changes the course of civilization, and the first bearer of that torch is the home. This chapter considers the purpose of education, the role of civilization and home, the art of living, and the spirit of the teacher together with the universe as a school. Learning does not end with the life in the flesh; the whole universe becomes one vast school.
ch21.s1.u1.k: The purpose of education is skill, wisdom, the realization of selfhood, and the attainment of spiritual values.
ch21.s1.u1.p: If education is seen merely as preparation for earning a living, its purpose stops at skill. The text begins with skill but sets out a ladder that rises through wisdom and self-realization to spiritual values. In the ideal state learning does not end with schooldays but continues throughout life, and citizens pursue a wisdom that sees into the meaning of human relations, the goals of living, and the glories of cosmic destiny. Education does not only make people useful; it makes them deep.
ch21.s1.u2.k: Education must move beyond success seeking to become world-wide, self-realizing, and cosmic grasping.
ch21.s1.u2.p: The text offers a sharp diagnosis of education as we know it: too long localistic, worshipful of force, inflating the ego, and chasing success. Its control has passed from clergy to lawyers and businessmen, but in the end it must go to philosophers and scientists who seek wisdom. When teachers become free beings and real leaders, education becomes the search for wisdom.
ch21.s1.u3.k: Education is the business of living, a lifelong ascent from knowledge to God-consciousness.
ch21.s1.u3.p: These seven levels show how wisdom grows. From knowing things we come to realize meanings and appreciate values; work becomes duty, goals become morality, the love of service becomes character, and at last cosmic insight opens into spiritual discernment. At the top stands the highest attainment open to the human mind, God-consciousness. The ladder of education leads finally to worship.
ch21.s2: The Torch of Civilization and the Home
ch21.s2.u1.k: Because the human baby is born without education, the training of the next generation changes the course of civilization.
ch21.s2.u1.p: Insects are born with the finished education of instinct, and live correspondingly narrow lives. Man is born knowing nothing, and for that very reason can learn without limit. Through social inheritance each generation stands on the shoulders of those who went before. In handing on that torch the home comes first, play and social life next, and the school last. The school cannot replace the home.
ch21.s2.u2.k: The most valuable part of a child's education and character training comes from parents at home.
ch21.s2.u2.p: The advanced nation described in the text and the schools of the Garden in Adam's day show the same principle. The school takes charge of socialization and practical training, while religious and sexual instruction remain the duty of home and parents, and fathers give child culture nearly as much attention as mothers do. The consistent view of this revelation is that the deepest values are handed on more at the family table than in the classroom.
ch21.s2.u3.k: The purpose of all education is the development of a majestic and well-balanced personality.
ch21.s2.u3.p: The statement that even secular education can serve a spiritual renaissance is significant. It does not call for more religion classes; it calls for teaching young people how to plan their lives and grow in character. When moral discipline is taught in place of self-gratification, religion can add its spiritual incentive on that foundation. Education and religion are not rivals but co-workers building the same personality.
ch21.s3.u1.k: The more complex civilization becomes, the more often mankind must learn anew the art of living.
ch21.s3.u1.p: Technical civilization advances rapidly, but the wisdom to live well within it does not follow automatically. When the art of living falls behind the technique of existence, people slip back into the simple urge to satisfy present desires. The faster an age changes, the more education must weigh the nurture of character and maturity above the mere addition of information.
ch21.s3.u2.k: The first step in solving any problem is to locate the difficulty and honestly acknowledge it.
ch21.s3.u2.p: Successful living is the art of mastering dependable techniques for solving common problems. Yet we usually fail to solve our problems not for lack of knowledge but because fear, conceit, and prejudice keep us from admitting them. True education therefore must do more than teach correct answers; it must cultivate the courage to stand before the truth.
ch21.s3.u3.k: Ability is inherited but skill is acquired, and doing one thing well is a source of life's satisfaction.
ch21.s3.u3.p: Inherited talent is only a starting point; skill is gained by honest toil. When we can do one thing expertly, life becomes real to us. This teaching reminds us that education is not only intellectual culture but the training of skilled workmanship. And the counsel to be a producer as well as a consumer tells us that learning should bear fruit in service to others.
ch21.s4: The Spirit of the Teacher and the Universe as a School
ch21.s4.u1.k: A true teacher guards the personality and self-respect of the learner.
ch21.s4.u1.p: The principles Jesus gave to those who taught the gospel apply to every teacher. Too much self-respect breeds pride, but its loss paralyzes the will. The aim of teaching is therefore to restore self-respect to those who have lost it and to restrain it in those who have too much. The counsel not merely to condemn wrongs but to recognize generously what is praiseworthy is an ancient wisdom of education.
ch21.s4.u2.k: The whole universe is one vast school, whose keynote is character acquired by enlightened experience.
ch21.s4.u2.p: Education does not end with the earthly career. From the mansion worlds to Salvington the ascending mortal is continually learning and being trained. The keynote of all this education is not the accumulation of knowledge but character. Teachers provide enlightenment, and one's station and work in the universe provide the opportunity for experience; when the two are wisely used together, character grows. Earthly education can take this principle as its pattern.
ch21.s4.u3.k: There are no short cuts to Paradise; what we fail to learn on earth must be learned later.
ch21.s4.u3.p: This statement is both a comfort and a warning. Lessons missed on earth are not lost; they are offered again under patient teachers. But such animal habits as procrastination, equivocation, and problem avoidance must at last be uprooted, and after the life in the flesh time no longer serves as a way of escape. There is, then, no reason to postpone today's learning.
ch21.qs1: Where along the seven levels of wisdom does my own education and present learning stand?
ch21.qs2: What is the most precious value I want to hand on to the next generation at home, and how am I handing it on?
ch21.qs3: What problem in my life am I refusing to acknowledge because of fear or conceit?
ch22.sub: Evolution's Supreme Glory, the First School of Love
ch22.sum: Marriage arose from mankind's adjustment to the two sexes, and its fruit, the home, is the supreme glory of the whole long and arduous evolutionary struggle. The Urantia Book does not sanctify marriage as a sacrament; it regards it as an essentially human institution, yet it says that the ideal mortal marriage is humanly sacred. Man and woman never fully understand each other, yet they need each other forever. The home is the founder of true morality and the place where the child first learns of God the Father. This chapter considers the nature of marriage, the complementarity of the sexes, the home as a school of morality, and the threats and hopes facing the home today.
ch22.s1: The Origin and Nature of Marriage
ch22.s1.u1.k: The home is the supreme glory of the whole evolutionary struggle and the chief civilizing agency.
ch22.s1.u1.p: Marriage cannot be explained by biological instinct alone. It is a social achievement, the fruit of mankind's long adjustment to the fact of two sexes, and from it the home arose. School, church, and state are all needed, but the child learns the essentials of living above all from home and neighborhood. Civilization depends less on the size of its institutions than on how soundly its homes function.
ch22.s1.u2.k: Marriage is man's most exalted institution, but it is essentially human.
ch22.s1.u2.p: Many religious traditions have regarded marriage as a sacrament joined by God. The Urantia Book corrects this view: the union of husband and wife is a material function of mortals on the evolutionary worlds and is not to be compared with the relation between God and man. Yet this does not make marriage a light matter. Sincere effort within marriage, like every other earnest endeavor, can yield much spiritual progress.
ch22.s1.u3.k: The ideal mortal marriage is humanly sacred, a glorious ideal that lures mankind toward greater happiness.
ch22.s1.u3.p: Seeing marriage as a human institution does not diminish its ideal. On the system capitals the Material Sons and Daughters actually embody that ideal, and earthly marriage grows toward it. Though that dream is seldom fully realized, marriage remains man's supreme dream of temporal ideality, ever luring mankind on to greater strivings for happiness.
ch22.s2.u1.k: Man and woman never fully understand each other, yet they need and complement each other forever.
ch22.s2.u1.p: The difference between the sexes is a gift to mankind before it is a cause of quarrels. Remarkably, the text says this difference does not end with mortal life but continues through the morontia and spirit careers, into Havona and even the Corps of the Finality. Two differing outlooks intrigue, stimulate, and help each other. Marriage is not an institution for erasing this difference but for adjusting it into co-operation.
ch22.s2.u2.k: The real test of marriage is the continuous intimacy that is inescapable in family life.
ch22.s2.u2.p: Courtship may begin in imagination and romance, but marriage is tested in the daily intimacy of living face to face. Two people raised to expect only self-gratification will find it hard to build a lifelong partnership of self-effacement, compromise, and devotion to children. The text points to the contradiction of a modern society that exalts love yet does little to prepare for marriage. Marriage is a matter of character more than of feeling.
ch22.s2.u3.k: Marriage is not an individualistic ideal but the evolving social partnership of a man and a woman.
ch22.s2.u3.p: As women's rights have grown, marriage is developing into an equal partnership founded on sexual fidelity, and this is a great advance. But the text warns against another extreme: a marriage that seeks to monopolize each other's whole personality and individuality is not healthy. Marriage is not only a private ideal of two people; it is also a public partnership functioning within the mores and laws of society.
ch22.s3: The Home as a School of Morality
ch22.s3.u1.k: Family life is the progenitor of true morality and the first revelation of the heavenly Parent's love.
ch22.s3.u1.p: In the home people learn patience, altruism, tolerance, and forbearance. The enforced association of living with differing personalities stabilizes character and stimulates its growth. But the deepest meaning of the home lies beyond this. Good parents come to understand the Creator's attitude toward his children, and to their children they become the first revelation of the love of the Paradise Parent. The brotherhood of man begins at home.
ch22.s3.u2.k: A child's first concept of the heavenly Father depends wholly on the earthly father.
ch22.s3.u2.p: Jesus' conversation with John Mark makes plain the spiritual weight of the home. The child gains his first impressions of the universe from his mother's care and forms his first picture of God through his father. The love and consistency of parents therefore shape a child's faith before any doctrinal instruction can. The first few years leave a deep mark on the whole of a life.
ch22.s3.u3.k: Any attempt to shift parental responsibility to state or church will prove suicidal to civilization.
ch22.s3.u3.p: In an industrial and urban age the cost of raising children rises, and children easily come to look like an economic burden. Yet the security of civilization depends on one generation's willingness to invest in the next, and that responsibility cannot be handed to other institutions. In place of patriarchal rule the text holds up the Andite family council, where every matter was discussed freely and frankly. A good home rests on brotherly co-operation.
ch22.s4: Threats and Hopes for the Home
ch22.s4.u1.k: The greatest threat to family life is the rising tide of self-gratification, the modern pleasure mania.
ch22.s4.u1.p: Marriage is the one institution that embraces all three motives of self-maintenance, self-perpetuation, and self-gratification. When the third swallows the other two, the home is shaken. The cravings of the soul cannot be satisfied by physical pleasure, and vanity and fashion have no power to build a home or rear children. This diagnosis speaks deeply to an age that sees marriage merely as a means to personal enjoyment.
ch22.s4.u2.k: Man deserves to enjoy himself, but not at the cost of the home.
ch22.s4.u2.p: The Urantia Book does not teach an asceticism that forbids pleasure; play, rest, and enjoyment are the rightful fruits of the long evolutionary struggle. But the goal of destiny must always be kept in view. If self-gratification destroys marriage and dissolves the home, the price paid is far too high, for the home is man's highest evolutionary achievement and the only hope for the survival of civilization.
ch22.s4.u3.k: The family stood at the center of Jesus' philosophy of life, and true religion and a wise home ennoble each other.
ch22.s4.u3.p: Jesus built his teaching about God in the language of the family: God is Father, men are his children and brothers to one another. He exalted family life as the highest human duty, yet he made it plain that family relationships must not interfere with religious obligations. And the love of a wise home and the devotion of true religion strengthen each other. The home is the first soil in which the gospel takes root.
ch22.qs1: How does seeing marriage not as a sacrament but as a humanly sacred institution change my view of marriage?
ch22.qs2: How has my concept of God been shaped by the home and parents I grew up with?
ch22.qs3: What could we change in our home today to nurture mutual devotion rather than self-gratification?
ch23.sub: Government for the People and the Sovereignty of Mankind
ch23.sum: The state is not an institution handed down from heaven but an evolutionary achievement that society has won from the ravages of war. The Urantia Book values what a government does above the form it takes, and it holds that no state can transcend the moral values of its citizens. The ideal state is moved by the loyalty of love, intelligent patriotism, and cosmic insight; it governs least and co-ordinates most. And if the world is to know lasting peace, it must pass beyond the illusion of unlimited national sovereignty to the sovereignty of mankind. This chapter considers the nature of the state, the ideal state, sovereignty and peace, and the twofold responsibility of being a son of the kingdom and a citizen of an earthly nation.
ch23.s1: The Origin and Nature of the State
ch23.s1.u1.k: The state is not of divine origin; it is a purely evolutionary institution.
ch23.s1.u1.p: Throughout history many states have presented themselves as sacred orders and demanded absolute loyalty from their citizens. The text strips away that myth. The state is an institution that survived the long struggle for group power, the net gain society has drawn from the sufferings of war. It is useful and necessary, but it is not divine. This recognition is the starting point of a balanced citizenship that neither worships nor despises the state.
ch23.s1.u2.k: The only divine feature of human government is its division into executive, legislative, and judicial domains.
ch23.s1.u2.p: The state itself is not divine, but one principle in it mirrors the way the universe is governed: the division of power into three branches that balance one another. After the long struggle over the concentration of power, it has become clear that evolutionary peoples are best governed by a balanced representative government. Beyond this, the form matters little so long as citizens grow toward self-control and service.
ch23.s1.u3.k: What a state does matters more than what it is, and no state can transcend the morals of its citizens.
ch23.s1.u3.p: Political debate often centers on the names of systems. The text shifts the focus: what matters is not what a state is but what it does. And in the end a government mirrors the leaders its citizens choose; ignorance and selfishness will bring down even the best institutions. A good state therefore begins with good citizens, and reform of the state cannot be separated from the moral growth of individuals.
ch23.s2.u1.k: The ideal state is moved by three impulses: the loyalty of love, intelligent patriotism, and cosmic insight.
ch23.s2.u1.p: The idea of a chosen people once bound tribes together and built nations, but intolerance is forever hostile to human progress. The ideal state rests not on exclusive patriotism but on a loyalty of love born of realizing the brotherhood of man. Patriotism is sound only when founded on wise ideals, and it must be guided by an insight that interprets the planet's needs from a cosmic viewpoint. Love of country finds its rightful place within the love of mankind.
ch23.s2.u2.k: The best state governs the least and co-ordinates the most.
ch23.s2.u2.p: A moral society aims to preserve the self-respect of its citizens and to give everyone an adequate opportunity for self-realization. This is achieved not by heavy control but by minimal regulation and broad co-ordination. Nor is the ideal state imposed from above; it comes as civic consciousness slowly grows. When people who once bore public office as a burden come to seek it as an honored privilege, civilization rises a level.
ch23.s2.u3.k: In the advanced state, political service is esteemed as the highest devotion of citizens.
ch23.s2.u3.p: Cynical contempt for politics ends by handing power to the incompetent and the selfish. The text paints a different picture: the wisest and noblest citizens make public office their highest ambition, and society gives its greatest honors to its public servants. People are free to form their own governments, and with that freedom comes the responsibility to choose those intellectually and morally fit to serve.
ch23.s3.u1.k: Citizens are not born for the government; government exists for the benefit of the people.
ch23.s3.u1.p: The revelators restate in modern terms the principles of sovereignty Jesus taught at Urmia. True sovereignty exists on only two levels: the spiritual free will of the individual and the collective sovereignty of mankind as a whole. Every group in between, whether tribe, people, or nation, has value only insofar as it furthers the welfare of the individual and of mankind. When the state makes itself the end, the order is inverted.
ch23.s3.u2.k: War is only a symptom; the real disease is the virus of unlimited national sovereignty.
ch23.s3.u2.p: Many efforts for peace concentrate on reducing arms and signing treaties. The text says these do not touch the root. Even if every weapon were taken away, nations that cling to the absoluteness of their sovereignty would fight with fists and stones. The problem lies not in the instruments but in the idea. To end war, mankind's very concept of sovereignty must change.
ch23.s3.u3.k: A world government of mankind does not surrender sovereignty but creates true sovereignty.
ch23.s3.u3.p: The phrase world government often stirs fear of a vast power that would swallow individual liberty. The text says the opposite. Present nations have never possessed a true sovereignty able to protect them from world war. When local matters are handled locally, national matters nationally, and international matters by a world government, the individual will enjoy far more freedom than now.
ch23.s3.u4.k: Liberty is a gift of civilization made possible by the enforcement of law.
ch23.s3.u4.p: Absolute liberty for one means absolute bondage for another. Liberty is therefore always relative, and it can be shared only under laws that secure equal freedom for all. Religion makes the brotherhood of mankind spiritually possible, but for that brotherhood to be realized in social, economic, and political life, the vessel of government is needed. Faith and institutions do not replace each other; they complete each other.
ch23.s4: The Kingdom of God and the Earthly State
ch23.s4.u1.k: The Most Highs rule in the kingdoms of men, and there is no chosen people.
ch23.s4.u1.p: Earthly politics may look like a purely human affair, but the text says the rule of the Most Highs stands above it. That rule favors no particular people; it is designed to bring the greatest good to the greatest number for the longest time. No nation, then, can present itself as God's sole instrument. The spiritual sovereignty of God takes precedence over every intermediate loyalty.
ch23.s4.u2.k: Because he is a son of the heavenly kingdom, the believer should be a better citizen of the earthly state.
ch23.s4.u2.p: Jesus taught that there is no conflict between sonship in the kingdom of God and citizenship on earth. The believer bears duties to man and to God, and willingly takes on a third, the service of the brotherhood. Faith does not draw us out of the world; it makes us more honest and devoted citizens. Yet we must refuse to worship rulers or to use the power of the state for spiritual ends.
ch23.qs1: How does my loyalty to my own country harmonize with my love for all mankind?
ch23.qs2: What can I do as a citizen toward a state that governs least and co-ordinates most?
ch23.qs3: In what ways does being a son or daughter of the kingdom make me a better citizen?
ch24.sub: Evil, Error, Sin, Iniquity, and the Price of Freedom
ch24.sum: The Urantia Book defines sin not as a vague state of fallenness but as a personal choice knowingly made against the will of God. The Gods do not create evil. Potential evil exists in a universe of differential levels of perfection, and sin is potential wherever imperfect beings can choose between good and evil. Freedom cannot escape the possibility of error, and in that very risk grows the goodness won through experience. Man is by nature imperfect but not necessarily a sinner, and he is not condemned for being born a descendant of Adam. This chapter considers the distinctions among evil, sin, and iniquity, the relation of freedom to evil, the nature of man, and a new understanding of sin together with God's attitude toward it.
ch24.s1: Evil, Error, Sin, and Iniquity Distinguished
ch24.s1.u1.k: The Gods do not create evil; the deliberate choice of evil constitutes sin.
ch24.s1.u1.p: The first step in understanding sin is to distinguish the words. Potential evil exists in time within a universe of differing levels of perfection, and error arises where truth and falsehood coexist. But sin is not a circumstance; it is a choice. The deliberate choice of evil is sin, and the persistent pursuit of sin and error is iniquity. This distinction corrects both the idea that God is the cause of evil and the idea that every imperfection is sin.
ch24.s1.u2.k: Evil is unconscious transgression, sin is knowing transgression, iniquity is persistent and determined transgression.
ch24.s1.u2.p: When Thomas asked what evil is, Jesus answered in three steps. The standard throughout is the Father's will, and the difference lies in the degree of awareness and intent. Transgression without knowing is evil but not yet sin. Knowing and deliberate transgression is sin, and when that refusal hardens into a final rejection of the Father's loving plan, it becomes iniquity. Sin is less a list of deeds than the direction of the heart toward God.
ch24.s1.u3.k: Sin is purposeful resistance to divine reality, a conscious choice to oppose spiritual progress.
ch24.s1.u3.p: Defined from the viewpoint of cosmic philosophy, sin concerns one's relation to reality. Error is a misunderstanding of reality, and evil a partial maladjustment to it, but sin is resistance to reality one knows. When that resistance becomes open and persistent, personality itself disintegrates toward cosmic insanity. Sin is finally a path of self-destruction, a cutting of oneself off from reality.
ch24.s2: Freedom and the Possibility of Evil
ch24.s2.u1.k: To be free, evolving man must be able to err.
ch24.s2.u1.p: Why did God not make a world without the possibility of mistakes? The text replies that such a world would be one without free intelligence. Perfect beings dwell in Havona, but evolving man must gain wisdom through experience, and a free but inexperienced intellect cannot be uniformly wise from the start. The possibility of mistaken judgment is the price of freedom; in itself it is not sin.
ch24.s2.u2.k: The power to choose good or evil is a universe reality, and God takes no one's freedom away.
ch24.s2.u2.p: Why evil and sin are permitted is a question that troubles every age. The text finds the answer in the reality of freedom. If freedom of choice is real, the possibility of wrong choice must be real too. Had God instantly prevented every rebellion, freedom would be no more than a symbolic ideal. The rulers of the universe deprive no one of this divine gift. The possibility of sin shows how seriously God takes freedom.
ch24.s2.u3.k: True liberty is the reward of progress; false liberty is a subtle deception of the error of time.
ch24.s2.u3.p: The greatest confusion left by the Lucifer rebellion concerned liberty. The rebellion promised freedom without any restraint, but such freedom is a self-destructive technique of cosmic existence. True liberty presupposes intelligence, maturity, fraternity, and fairness, and only a freedom that regards one's duties to neighbor and universe endures. Liberty is not the power to do as I please; it is the capacity to be ever more deeply related to reality.
ch24.s3: Man Is Evil but Not Necessarily a Sinner
ch24.s3.u1.k: Imperfection of natural endowment is not sin; sin is a conscious attitude of rebellion.
ch24.s3.u1.p: Man is born with imperfect tendencies inherited from his animal origins, yet these are only the starting point of a long ascent, not grounds for condemnation. Jesus clearly distinguished between being exposed to evil and being a sinner. Evil is inherent in the natural order of this world, but sin is an attitude brought in by those who knew the spiritual light and chose darkness. This distinction gives man hope rather than shame.
ch24.s3.u2.k: Man is not a being fallen from perfection but one ascending toward divine perfection.
ch24.s3.u2.p: The idea that mankind began with perfect ancestors and fell through sin long dominated theology. Jesus reverses this picture: man begins low and rises toward God and divine perfection. Seen this way, salvation is not recovering a lost status but advancing toward a destiny not yet attained.
ch24.s3.u3.k: Sin is wholly personal, and no one suffers spiritual loss because of another's sin.
ch24.s3.u3.p: Caligastia's rebellion and Adam's default left deep wounds on this world: intellectual, social, and spiritual progress was retarded, and everyone born since has suffered temporal handicaps. Yet no one's eternal destiny has been jeopardized by them. The moral guilt and spiritual consequences of sin are wholly personal. This corrects the doctrine of original sin and at the same time reminds each person of responsibility for his own choices.
ch24.s4: Sin Redefined and the Attitude of God
ch24.s4.u1.k: Sin must be redefined as deliberate disloyalty to Deity.
ch24.s4.u1.p: The ancients could be sure of God's favor only through sacrifice, but modern man needs a new understanding. The text redefines sin not as the breaking of a taboo but as a matter of loyalty to God. Undecided partial loyalty, divided loyalty, loyalty dying through indifference, and loyalty given to godless ideals are its stages. A sense of guilt is not itself sin; without conscious disloyalty to Deity there is no real sin.
ch24.s4.u2.k: The capacity to recognize guilt is a mark not of man's baseness but of his potential greatness.
ch24.s4.u2.p: Guilt is often regarded only as a crushing burden. The text reads it differently: the ability to recognize wrong as wrong is a transcendent excellence given to man and not to animals. The feeling of unworthiness is meant not to cast us down but to be the first stimulus toward the conquests of faith. Honest confession does not erase consequences, but it opens the door to spiritual growth.
ch24.s4.u3.k: The love of God saves the sinner; the law of God destroys the sin.
ch24.s4.u3.p: God is a person, and so he loves persons. Sin is not a person, nor is it a spiritual reality; God therefore takes no personal attitude toward it but deals with its existence through justice alone. Thus divine love and divine justice do not collide: love holds fast to the sinner, who has eternal possibilities, while law does away with sin, which is unreal. Unless a person finally identifies himself with sin, love has the last word.
ch24.qs1: How have I distinguished between imperfection and sin, and how does this chapter's distinction change the way I see myself?
ch24.qs2: If sin is disloyalty to God, at what stage does my own loyalty stand today?
ch24.qs3: Have I known a time when guilt led me not into despair but into growth in faith?
ch25.sub: The Mission and Default of the Biologic Uplifters
ch25.sum: The Adam and Eve of the Urantia Book are not the first human beings of myth but a Material Son and Daughter sent from Jerusem, the system capital, to uplift the evolutionary races biologically and to quicken their culture. They undertook an almost hopeless task on a world wounded and isolated by rebellion, and in loneliness and impatience they fell into default by trying to outrun the divine plan through a short cut. Yet there was no "fall of man." Mankind was in fact uplifted by their contribution, and their transgression was an error of judgment, not deliberate rebellion. This chapter considers the mission of the biologic uplifters, the course of the default, a reinterpretation of the doctrine of the fall, and the story of repentance and restoration.
ch25.s1.u1.k: Adam and Eve are a Material Son and Daughter sent to uplift the evolutionary races, the material gift of the Creator Son.
ch25.s1.u1.p: The Urantia Book presents Adam and Eve not as the first ancestors of mankind but as an order of sonship that comes according to a set universe plan. When primitive man reaches the limit of natural evolutionary development, the System Sovereign sends a pair of biologic uplifters. With the Planetary Prince they remain on that world throughout its evolution, upstepping the races and quickening culture. They are the material gift of the Creator Son to the inhabited worlds.
ch25.s1.u2.k: On normal worlds the Garden of Eden functions for ages as the pattern and center of world culture.
ch25.s1.u2.p: On worlds where the mission of Adam and Eve succeeds, the Garden of Eden remains for ages a cultural center and the social pattern of planetary life. Even in early times, while the violet people live relatively apart, their schools receive suitable students from the world races, and the industries of the Garden open new channels of commerce. This is the original shape of the divine plan. Only by keeping this normal picture in mind can we see, in reading Urantia's story, what was lost and what remained.
ch25.s1.u3.k: Adam and Eve took up an almost hopeless task on a planet isolated by rebellion.
ch25.s1.u3.p: Urantia was a world placed in spiritual isolation by the rebellion of its Planetary Prince, Caligastia. Adam and Eve arrived where nothing was ready for the proclamation of the brotherhood of man, a world groping in spiritual darkness, its confusion worse confounded. The text says no Adam was ever assigned to a more difficult world. In judging their failure we must remember these conditions first.
ch25.s2.u1.k: The default began not in evil intent but in a wish to hasten the good, born of loneliness and impatience.
ch25.s2.u1.p: Isolated, with no way to consult their superiors, Adam and Eve gradually lost heart. Then Serapatatia, a Nodite leader, urged a plan: if a leader of part violet descent could be born to the Nodites, those peoples would be bound more closely to the Garden. The idea was soberly and honestly considered to be for the good of the world. The tragedy came not from malice but from good intentions, from choosing a short cut instead of waiting.
ch25.s2.u2.k: The warning against mixing good and evil meant not to mingle the divine plan with human devising.
ch25.s2.u2.p: The story of the tree of knowledge of good and evil gains new meaning here. Good is carrying out the divine plan, sin is deliberate transgression of the divine will, and evil is the misapplication of plans that produces disharmony. Adam and Eve were warned again and again: on the day they mingled good and evil, they would become as the mortals of the realm. Even a good purpose, mixed with wrong methods, breeds confusion.
ch25.s2.u3.k: On the way to Paradise nothing is gained by trying to circumvent the divine plan through short cuts.
ch25.s2.u3.p: The text says that had Adam and Eve been a little more patient, they would eventually have succeeded. But Eve listened to the subtle propaganda of personal liberty. The lesson applies to every ascender: the divine plan may seem slow, yet it is the surest way, and impatient devising ends in a longer detour. Patience is a central virtue of spiritual maturity.
ch25.s3: There Was No Fall of Man
ch25.s3.u1.k: There was no fall of man; mankind was in fact uplifted by Adam's bestowal.
ch25.s3.u1.p: The doctrine that mankind fell through Adam's transgression and inherited a sinful nature has been a great pillar of Christian theology. The Urantia Book plainly denies it. Adam and Eve fell from the high estate of Material Sonship to the status of mortals, but that was not the fall of man. Human history is a story of progressive evolution, and the Adamic bestowal left the peoples of the world greatly improved over their former biologic condition.
ch25.s3.u2.k: Adam should not be regarded as the cause of a curse on the human race.
ch25.s3.u2.p: Adam and Eve have long been blamed as the authors of every human misfortune. The text assesses them more fairly. They broke their covenant and lost their status, yet their contribution did much to advance the civilization of Urantia, and the high councils do not regard their mission as a total loss. Heaven's way of seeing is to recognize the good that the failed have left behind rather than to condemn them.
ch25.s3.u3.k: Perfection is not our origin but our eternal goal, and a personal, progressive universe is glorious.
ch25.s3.u3.p: The revelator who recounts the tragedy of Eden does not see the very possibility of mistakes as a flaw in the universe. The universe was not created perfect; perfection is not the starting point but the goal to be reached. That disagreement and misunderstanding are possible is evidence that personality is alive in the universe. This confession, that a personal and progressive universe is more glorious than a mechanically perfect one, places failure within the context of growth.
ch25.s4.u1.k: The transgression of Adam and Eve was an error of judgment, and their repentance was accepted.
ch25.s4.u1.p: Adam and Eve did not stage a conscious and deliberate rebellion. Their wrong was an error of judgment, and they sincerely repented. Remarkably, after being reduced to mortal status they experienced the indwelling of a Thought Adjuster, which they had never had before. Human status coupled with sincere repentance had made it possible for an Adjuster to indwell them. A new path began at the very place of failure.
ch25.s4.u2.k: Michael remembered the loyal hearts of those who defaulted and promised to call them forth.
ch25.s4.u2.p: The only personal message Adam and Eve ever received from Michael is the warmest passage in this story. The sovereign of the universe remembered not only their failure but the desire of their hearts to be loyal to the Father's will. God does not judge people by outcomes alone; he looks at motives and longings. This promise tells everyone who has failed that hope remains so long as the heart is turned toward God.
ch25.s4.u3.k: Raised in a special resurrection, Adam and Eve became ascending citizens and still serve Urantia.
ch25.s4.u3.p: The story of Adam and Eve does not end in failure. They fell asleep trusting the promise of resurrection and awoke on the mansion worlds in a special resurrection. They passed quickly through the worlds of progressive ascension, attained citizenship on Jerusem, and returned to their home planet as members of a different order of universe personalities. Today they are among the twenty-four counselors who serve Urantia. This story of restoration is a vivid testimony that salvation is open to all.
ch25.qs1: If I have ever taken a short cut instead of the appointed way in order to reach a good goal, what came of it?
ch25.qs2: How does the teaching that there was no fall of man change my thinking about human nature and salvation?
ch25.qs3: How does the fact that God looks at the desire of the heart more than at outcomes help me view my own failures?
